skill.name: Lead with the dependent clause for effect
skill.why: Clause order picks what the reader meets first. Choose it on purpose.
skill.how: Move the dependent clause to the front. Add a comma. Don't add and, but or so.

steps.say: Same two clauses, two orders. Both are correct.

show.nudge: 'The floor gave way' makes sense alone. That's the main clause. Try the other part.

show.text: as Zed reached the last level.

steps.win: Yes! Main clause first: big news straight away.

steps.say: Now flip it. Dependent clause first, then a comma.

show.text: As Zed reached the last level,

steps.ask: What does leading with the dependent clause do here?

options.text: You wait, and the big moment lands last.
It makes the sentence shorter.
options.reason: Count the words. Same words, same length. What do you meet first now?

options.text: It explains why the floor broke.
options.reason: Neither order says why. What do you meet first now, and what last?

steps.win: Yes! You wait, then the floor drops.

steps.say: It's not only for suspense. Signs do it too.
steps.ask: Why does the sign start with the if part?

options.text: The dependent clause must always go first.
options.reason: Both orders are correct. 'Stand very still if you see a snake' works too.

options.text: You find out when the rule applies first.
It hides the instruction.
options.reason: The instruction is still there. What do you find out first?

steps.win: Yes! Situation first, then instruction. Order it for the reader.

steps.say: Careful! Zed added an extra joining word. Very common mistake.

show.nudge: The although clause is fine. It already does the joining. Look after the comma.
'It knocked Zed out' is the main clause. It has to stay. Look just before it.

steps.ask: Tap the word that has to go.
steps.win: Yes! 'Although' already joins them. No extra 'but' or 'so'.

steps.say: Careful! Check the opener for a doer and a verb.
steps.ask: Does this sentence lead with a dependent clause?

options.text: Yes: it starts with 'after'.
options.reason: 'After' can start a phrase too. Can you find a verb in 'after lunch'?

options.text: Yes: it has a comma.
options.reason: A phrase can have a comma too. Does 'after lunch' have a doer and a verb?

options.text: No: 'after lunch' has no verb.

steps.win: Right! 'After lunch' has no verb, so it's a phrase.

steps.say: Zed wants the bat to be the last surprise.
steps.ask: Which version saves the bat for last, with the right punctuation?

options.text: A bat flew out when Zed opened the chest.
options.reason: The bat comes first, so the surprise is gone. What should the reader meet last?

options.text: When Zed opened the chest, a bat flew out.
When Zed opened the chest a bat flew out.
options.reason: Look after 'chest'. Leading with a dependent clause needs a comma there.

steps.win: Yes! The when clause, then a comma, then the bat.

terms.means: A clause that starts with a word like when, because or if. It can't stand alone.
A clause that makes sense on its own. Every sentence needs one.
And and but join two whole thoughts. When, because, although make one part need the other.
A group of words with no verb, like 'after lunch'.

examples.text: As Zed reached the last level,

card.test: Lead with what the reader should meet first. Then a comma. No extra 'and', 'but' or 'so'.

weDo.prompt: Which version leads with the dependent clause?
weDo.hint: Which version makes you wait for the main clause?
weDo.success: 'When the whistle blew' comes first, then a comma, then the main clause.

options.text: When the whistle blew, the crowd went silent.
The crowd went silent when the whistle blew.
options.reason: This one leads with the main clause. The dependent clause comes last.

options.text: The whistle blew, and the crowd went silent.
options.reason: This joins two main clauses with and. There's no dependent clause to lead with.

weDo.prompt: Build the sign so the condition comes first.
weDo.hint: Which part tells you when the rule applies?
weDo.success: The if part comes first, so everyone knows when to move before they're told where to go.

accept: If the alarm rings, walk straight to the oval.
body.reason: Which part tells you when the rule applies? Start with that, then the instruction after the comma.

creature.name: Frillip
creature.blurb: A frill-necked lizard that flares its frill before it makes its move, so you're already on the edge of your seat when the main action lands.

write.ask: Join these into one sentence that leads with the dependent clause, so the surprise lands last.
given: Mo was halfway through his magic trick.
checks: My sentence starts with the dependent clause
A comma comes before the main clause
write.model: Just as Mo was halfway through his magic trick, the lights went out.

encounters.frame: A Frillip is flaring its frill at Tully's match report.
encounters.prompt: Which version leads with the dependent clause?
encounters.success: 'Before the siren went' comes first. A comma marks where the main clause starts.

options.text: Before the siren went, Tully kicked the goal.
Tully kicked the goal before the siren went.
options.reason: This leads with the main clause. The dependent clause is at the end.

options.text: Tully kicked the goal, and then the siren went.
options.reason: And joins two main clauses. There's no dependent clause here.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote her rescue notes two ways. The Frillip wants them sorted.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to the right pile.
encounters.success: Same clauses, different order. Leading with the dependent clause puts the when or why first.

items.text: When the possum hissed, Wren jumped.
items.reason: 'When the possum hissed' comes first, so it leads with the dependent clause.

items.text: Wren jumped when the possum hissed.
items.reason: 'Wren jumped' comes first. That's the main clause.

items.text: Because the joey was cold, we wrapped it up.
items.reason: The because part comes first, so it leads with the dependent clause.

items.text: We wrapped the joey up because it was cold.
items.reason: 'We wrapped the joey up' comes first. That's the main clause.

encounters.frame: Mo's cooking diary is in pieces again.
encounters.prompt: Tap the pieces in order. Lead with the dependent clause.
encounters.success: Leading with 'While Mo was cooking' sets the scene. Then the smoke alarm lands at the end, like a punchline.

accept: While Mo was cooking, the smoke alarm went off.
body.reason: Which part can't stand alone? That's the dependent clause, and it goes first.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing a space story. He wants you to wait for the big moment.
encounters.prompt: Which version leads with the dependent clause, so you wait for the eyeball?
encounters.success: Leading with 'As the hatch creaked open' makes you wait. Then the eyeball lands at the end.

options.text: As the hatch creaked open, we met a giant eyeball.
We met a giant eyeball as the hatch creaked open.
options.reason: This gives away the eyeball first, so there's nothing left to wait for.

options.text: We stared as the hatch creaked open on a giant eyeball.
options.reason: This ends on the eyeball too, but it leads with the main clause, 'We stared'.

encounters.frame: The Frillip found a spooky sentence in pieces under the old piano.
encounters.prompt: Tap the pieces in order so the sentence leads with the dependent clause.
encounters.success: The when part goes first and sets the scene. Then the piano surprises you at the end.

tiles: The old piano began to play
the old piano began to play.
accept: When the clock struck twelve, the old piano began to play.
body.reason: Start with the part that leaves you waiting. The main clause comes after the comma.

encounters.frame: Zed's game guide has three tips. The Frillip only likes one of them.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that leads with a dependent clause.
encounters.success: 'If you fall in the lava' comes first, so you get the warning before the bad news.

parts.tap: Collect the gold key first.
parts.reason: This is just one main clause. There's no dependent clause to lead with.

parts.tap: If you fall in the lava, you lose a life.
The dragon sleeps until you ring the bell.
parts.reason: This leads with the main clause. 'Until you ring the bell' comes at the end.

encounters.frame: The Frillip is reading the lifeguard's sign at the beach.
encounters.text: If you see a bluebottle, don't touch it.
encounters.prompt: Why does the sign lead with the dependent clause?
encounters.success: Leading with the if part tells you the situation first, so the instruction makes sense the moment you read it.

options.text: So you know the situation before you get the instruction.
Because a dependent clause always has to go first.
options.reason: Dependent clauses can go first or last. The sign writer chose to put this one first.

options.text: So the instruction is the very first thing that you read.
options.reason: The instruction comes last here. The situation, seeing a bluebottle, comes first.

encounters.frame: The school band's concert review is a mess. The Frillip is sorting the sentences.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to the right pile.
encounters.success: Starts with an after, although or until clause, then a comma? It leads with the dependent clause.

items.text: After the drummer counted in, the whole band started at once.
items.reason: 'After the drummer counted in' comes first, then the main clause.

items.text: The crowd went wild when the guitarist jumped off the stage.
items.reason: 'The crowd went wild' comes first. That's the main clause.

items.text: Although she had a sore throat, the singer hit every note.
items.reason: The although part comes first, so it leads with the dependent clause.

items.text: The lights went out just as the chorus began.
items.reason: 'The lights went out' is the main clause, and it comes first.

items.text: Until the last note faded, nobody moved.
items.reason: 'Until the last note faded' comes first, then the main clause.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing a warning for his robot's door. He wants the condition first.
encounters.prompt: Build Gus's warning so the condition comes first.
encounters.success: The unless part comes first, so visitors know about the password before they reach the door.

tiles: the robot won't open the door.
The robot won't open the door
accept: Unless you say the password, the robot won't open the door.
body.reason: Which part is the condition? Put it first, then the main clause after the comma.

encounters.frame: Mo moved his dependent clause to the front but forgot to take out the old joining word.
encounters.prompt: Tap the part with the extra joining word, then choose a fix.
encounters.success: Although has already done the joining. After the comma, the main clause starts straight away: it tasted like cardboard.

parts.tap: amazing
parts.reason: Amazing is fine. Look for a second joining word after the comma.

parts.tap: but it
cardboard
parts.reason: Cardboard is the funny part, and it's fine. Look for a second joining word after the comma.

options.text: it
and it
options.reason: And is another joining word. Although has already done the joining, so you don't need a second one.

options.text: so it
options.reason: So is another joining word, and it gives the wrong meaning. Although has already done the joining.

encounters.frame: Wren wants readers to know when it happened before they find out what happened.
encounters.prompt: Which version does that?
encounters.success: 'After the storm had passed' sets the scene first. Then the owl in the letterbox is the surprise.

options.text: After the storm had passed, a baby owl was sitting in our letterbox.
A baby owl was sitting in our letterbox after the storm had passed.
options.reason: This tells you what happened first and leaves the when until the end.

options.text: A baby owl, after the storm had passed, was sitting in our letterbox.
options.reason: This starts with the owl, which is what happened. The when is squeezed into the middle.

encounters.frame: Maxx Vantablack says Tully's report is boring. The Frillip has found the line that proves him wrong.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that leads with a dependent clause.
encounters.success: 'Just as the final siren sounded' comes first, so you wait for the winning goal at the very end.

parts.tap: We were winning by a goal when the rain started.
parts.reason: This has a dependent clause, but it comes last. 'We were winning by a goal' leads.

parts.tap: Our captain slipped over in the mud.
parts.reason: This is just one main clause. There's no dependent clause to lead with.

parts.tap: Just as the final siren sounded, Jai kicked the winning goal from fifty metres.

encounters.frame: Zed has four drafts of the scariest line in his story. The Frillip is shaking.
encounters.prompt: Which version leads with the dependent clause and keeps the cold hand a secret until the end?
encounters.success: Leading with the as clause keeps you creeping down the hallway. The cold hand comes last.

options.text: As Zed crept down the dark hallway towards the humming noise, a cold hand grabbed his ankle.
A cold hand grabbed Zed's ankle as he crept down the dark hallway towards the humming noise.
options.reason: The cold hand comes straight away, so there's nothing left to wait for.

options.text: Zed crept down the dark hallway until a cold hand grabbed his ankle.
options.reason: The cold hand comes late here too, but this leads with the main clause, 'Zed crept down the dark hallway'.

options.text: A cold hand, as Zed crept down the dark hallway, grabbed his ankle.
options.reason: You meet the cold hand before anything else, so it's not a secret for long.

encounters.frame: Tully's holiday diary has a sentence he's very proud of.
encounters.text: Although the ferry had left and the last bus was gone, the twins made it home for dinner.
encounters.prompt: Why does this sentence lead with the dependent clause?
encounters.success: The problems pile up first, so you expect the twins to be stuck. Then the good news lands.

options.text: It lists the problems first, so the good news at the end surprises you.
It tells you exactly how the twins managed to get home in time for dinner.
options.reason: The sentence never says how they got home. It only says they made it.

options.text: A sentence with although must always start with although.
options.reason: Although can go in the middle too: 'The twins made it home, although the ferry had left.'

options.text: It makes the sentence shorter.
options.reason: Moving the clause doesn't change the number of words. It changes what you read first.

encounters.frame: The marine park's fact cards are mixed up. The Frillip wants three piles.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to the right pile.
encounters.success: A dependent clause has a doer and verb. 'During the storm' has no verb, so it's a phrase.

items.text: When the tide turned, the seals slid back into the water.
items.reason: 'When the tide turned' comes first, then the main clause.

items.text: The seals slid back into the water when the tide turned.
items.reason: The main clause comes first, and 'when the tide turned' comes last.

items.text: The tide turned, and the seals slid back into the water.
items.reason: Both parts can stand alone, joined by and. Neither one is dependent.

items.text: Because the coral was bleached, the divers took photos for the scientists.
items.reason: The because part comes first, so the dependent clause leads.

items.text: The divers took photos for the scientists because the coral was bleached.
items.reason: The because part comes at the end, after the main clause.

items.text: During the storm, the boat rocked wildly.
items.reason: 'During the storm' has no verb, so it's a phrase. There's only one clause here.

encounters.frame: Gus has two sentences for his science diary. He wants the reason first, so the gross bit lands last.
encounters.text: The fridge had been off for a week. The yoghurt had grown a fur coat.
encounters.prompt: Tap the pieces in order to join these. Lead with the dependent clause.
encounters.success: The reason comes first and you start to worry. Then the fur coat lands at the end. Gross.

tiles: The fridge had been off for a week,
and the yoghurt had grown a fur coat.
the fridge had been off for a week,
the yoghurt had grown a fur coat.
accept: Because the fridge had been off for a week, the yoghurt had grown a fur coat.
body.reason: Pick the joining word that gives a reason. After the comma, the main clause starts straight away.

encounters.frame: The Frillip spotted a sentence on the footy club noticeboard with one joining word too many.
encounters.prompt: Tap the part with the extra joining word, then choose a fix.
encounters.success: Because already joins the two ideas, so after the comma the main clause starts straight away.

parts.tap: waterlogged
parts.reason: Waterlogged is fine. Look for an extra joining word after the comma.

parts.tap: so the umpires
called off
parts.reason: Called off is fine. Look for an extra joining word after the comma.

options.text: the umpires
and the umpires
options.reason: And adds a second joining word. Because has already linked the two ideas.

options.text: but the umpires
options.reason: But adds a second joining word and suggests a surprise that isn't there.

options.text: then the umpires
options.reason: Then isn't needed after a because clause. The comma already shows where the main clause starts.

encounters.frame: Indi's gallery tour has four sentences. Only one leads with a dependent clause.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that leads with a dependent clause.
encounters.success: 'Once everyone could see it' has a doer and verb, but can't stand alone. It's a dependent clause.

parts.tap: After lunch, Indi unveiled her mural.
parts.reason: 'After lunch' has no verb, so it's a phrase, not a clause.

parts.tap: Slowly, the curtain slid to the floor.
parts.reason: Slowly is a single word that says how. It isn't a clause.

parts.tap: Once everyone could see it, the room went quiet.
Then someone sneezed, and the whole wall of paint slid off.
parts.reason: This leads with a main clause, 'someone sneezed'. Then is just a time word.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing about the night the comet appeared. The Frillip is helping him choose his next sentence.
encounters.text: For six days, thick cloud hid the comet from the observatory.
encounters.prompt: Which next sentence picks up from the cloud before it shows the comet?
encounters.success: Leading with 'when the cloud finally cleared' links back to the cloud. Then the comet lands at the end.

options.text: The whole town saw the comet blaze across the sky when the cloud finally cleared.
options.reason: This is correct, but it jumps to the comet first. The cloud only comes back at the end.

options.text: When the cloud finally cleared, the whole town saw the comet blaze across the sky.
Although the cloud finally cleared, the whole town saw the comet blaze across the sky.
options.reason: Although signals a surprise, but a clear sky is exactly when you'd expect to see a comet.

options.text: When the cloud finally cleared, and the whole town saw the comet blaze across the sky.
options.reason: The extra 'and' leaves no main clause. After the comma, the main clause should start straight away.

encounters.frame: A music critic wrote this about a young pianist. The Frillip wants to know why it works.
encounters.text: Even though the hall was half empty and the piano was out of tune, the pianist played like a star.
encounters.prompt: What does leading with the dependent clause do here?
encounters.success: The problems come first, so you expect a flop. Then the brilliant playing lands at the end as the payoff.

options.text: It sets up the problems first, so the brilliant playing feels like a payoff.
It shows that the half-empty hall was the most important news of the whole evening.
options.reason: The main clause is about the pianist, not the hall. The hall is the setting-up part.

options.text: It explains why the piano was out of tune.
options.reason: The sentence never says why the piano was out of tune.

options.text: It tells the reader the pianist played badly.
options.reason: 'Played like a star' means she played brilliantly, not badly.

encounters.frame: Gus is commentating the robot championships. The Frillip wants his openers sorted.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to the right pile.
encounters.success: Judge the opener by its verb, not its first word. 'After' and 'until' can start a phrase too.

items.text: As soon as the buzzer sounded, both robots charged at the cone.
items.reason: 'As soon as the buzzer sounded' has a doer and a verb, but it can't stand alone.

items.text: After the buzzer, both robots charged at the cone.
items.reason: 'After' can start a clause, but 'after the buzzer' has no verb. It's a phrase.

items.text: Until the final, nobody had beaten Unit 9.
items.reason: 'Until' often starts a clause, but 'until the final' has no verb. It's a phrase.

items.text: Although its arm had fallen off, the little robot kept pushing.
items.reason: 'Although its arm had fallen off' has a doer and a verb, but it can't stand alone.

items.text: Unit 9 kept spinning until its battery died.
items.reason: 'Unit 9 kept spinning' comes first and makes sense alone. The until clause comes last.

items.text: Whenever the arena lights flicker, the robots freeze in place.
items.reason: 'Whenever the arena lights flicker' has a doer and a verb, but it can't stand alone.

items.text: The champion robot reversed into the wall, and the crowd gasped.
items.reason: It has a comma, but 'the champion robot reversed into the wall' makes sense alone, and it leads.

encounters.frame: The zoo newsletter has four lines about the runaway emu. Maxx Vantablack says they all lead with a dependent clause.
encounters.prompt: Tap the only line that really leads with a dependent clause.
